```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
```

A [Qualtrics](https://www.qualtrics.com/) response download names its
columns with identifiers such as `QID12_3_TEXT`, and what each identifier
means is spread across several nested metadata objects: questions, choices,
matrix items, loops, embedded data and scoring rules. Before any analysis,
every column has to be matched back to that metadata, renamed, labelled and
documented.

qualtdict does that mapping for you. From the survey metadata it builds a
Variable Dictionary, one table describing every exported response column,
which you can inspect, validate and share as a codebook. It then applies the
dictionary to the responses downloaded through
[qualtRics](https://github.com/ropensci/qualtRics), so that every column
carries its variable name and labels.

The authors and contributors for this R package are not affiliated with
Qualtrics, and Qualtrics does not offer support for this R package.

## The workflow

1. `dict_generate()` builds a Variable Dictionary from the survey metadata.
2. `dict_validate()` reports Validation Findings in the dictionary.
3. `survey_fetch_labelled()` downloads the responses and applies the
   dictionary, returning Labelled Survey Data.
4. `dict_split_blocks()` and `survey_split_blocks()` give one view per
   Survey Block.

Steps 1 and 3 read your survey from Qualtrics and need API credentials.
Your institution must allow API access, and it must be enabled for your
account; the person who manages your Qualtrics account can give you your
API token and base URL. Store them once with `qualtrics_api_credentials()`,
which qualtdict re-exports from qualtRics:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
library(qualtdict)

qualtrics_api_credentials(
  api_key = "<YOUR-QUALTRICS_API_KEY>",
  base_url = "<YOUR-QUALTRICS_BASE_URL>",
  install = TRUE
)
```

## The example survey

This vignette uses `glad_example`, an example bundled with the package. It
holds the metadata of a subset of the GLAD Study sign-up survey (four
demographic questions, the PHQ-9 and GAD-7 blocks, six embedded data fields
and two scoring variables), 20 synthetic responses, and the objects qualtdict
produces from them.

```{r}
library(qualtdict)

names(glad_example)
```

For your own survey, the calls below would download the metadata and the
responses from Qualtrics. They are not run here; for the example survey they
return exactly `glad_example$dictionary` and
`glad_example$labelled_survey_data`, which the rest of this vignette uses.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
survey_id <- "SV_XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX"

dict <- dict_generate(survey_id, variable_name = "question_name")
survey_dat <- survey_fetch_labelled(dict)
```

```{r}
dict <- glad_example$dictionary
survey_dat <- glad_example$labelled_survey_data
```

## The Variable Dictionary

```{r}
dict
```

Each row describes one downloaded response column, or one response level of
it. The columns are:

- `response_column_id`: the column name in the downloaded Qualtrics response
  file. This is how the dictionary is matched to your data.
- `row_source`: what the column comes from (see below).
- `qid`: the Qualtrics question the column belongs to, such as `QID1125`.
  One question can produce many response columns.
- `question_name`: the question name set in the Qualtrics survey editor.
- `variable_name`: the name the column gets in Labelled Survey Data. It is
  unique and safe for export.
- `block`: the Survey Block the question belongs to.
- `question` and `item`: the question text and, for matrix and multi-column
  questions, the text of the row or choice.
- `level` and `label`: a response value and its label. A column with
  response options takes one row per option.
- `type`, `selector`, `sub_selector` and `content_type`: the Qualtrics
  question type and its settings.

`variable_name = "question_name"` builds `variable_name` from the Qualtrics
Question Name, repaired where needed so that every name is unique and
export-safe. The original `question_name` stays in the dictionary.

A multi-select question gets one response column per choice, and a choice
with a text box gets an extra `_TEXT` column:

```{r}
dict[
  which(dict$qid == "QID1147"),
  c("response_column_id", "variable_name", "level", "label")
]
```

A matrix question gets one response column per item, each with the scale's
levels:

```{r}
dict[
  which(dict$qid == "QID127303424" & dict$level == "0"),
  c("response_column_id", "variable_name", "item")
]
```

### Row sources

Most rows come from survey questions, but Qualtrics also exports columns that
are defined elsewhere in the survey. `row_source` says which:

- `question`: a response to a survey question.
- `embedded_data`: an Embedded Data Field set in the Survey Flow.
- `scoring`: a Scoring Variable computed by Qualtrics scoring.
- `text_analysis`: a Text-analysis Sidecar added by Qualtrics text analysis
  of a text response. The example survey has none.

```{r}
table(dict$row_source)

dict[
  dict$row_source != "question",
  c("response_column_id", "row_source", "variable_name", "question")
]
```

## Validation Findings

`dict_validate()` returns a list with two components: `validation_findings`,
one row per finding, and `level_label_pairs`, the distinct level-label
codings of the survey's questions.

```{r}
validation <- dict_validate(dict)
names(validation)

validation$validation_findings[, c(
  "finding", "severity", "response_column_id", "original_candidate",
  "variable_name", "reason"
)]
```

Each finding has a `severity`:

- **Suggestive** findings are worth a look but leave the column's data and
  identity sound. All findings here are of this kind: matrix items and
  multi-select choices share one Question Name, so their variable names are
  numbered, and the hyphens in `PHQ-9` and `GAD-7` are replaced so the
  scoring variables get export-safe names.
- **Definite** findings mean the column cannot be interpreted or identified
  reliably: duplicate or unsafe final variable names, or level-label codings
  that are not one-to-one, such as two choices sharing one response code.

A clean result is a consistency check, not proof that the survey itself is
correct.

`dict_assert_valid()` is the strict version for the definite findings that
make labelling wrong or impossible, the Export-blocking level-label codings.
It returns the dictionary invisibly when there are none, and raises an error
naming the offending columns otherwise. The example dictionary passes:

```{r}
dict_assert_valid(dict)
```

`survey_fetch_labelled()` runs this check before it downloads anything, so a
dictionary that cannot be labelled fails before the download.

## Labelled Survey Data

```{r}
dplyr::glimpse(survey_dat)
```

Export Variables are renamed from `response_column_id` to `variable_name`.
By default `survey_fetch_labelled()` also keeps `externalDataReference`,
`startDate` and `endDate`, and appends the response metadata columns
`recordedDate`, `ResponseId` and `Progress`.

Choice columns carry their response options as value labels, and text and
numeric columns carry the question text as a variable label:

```{r}
attr(survey_dat$DEM.COR.1.0, "labels")
attr(survey_dat$DEM.AGE.1.0, "label")
```

Packages that read these attributes, such as sjlabelled, can use them
directly, for example to turn a coded column into a factor:

```{r}
table(sjlabelled::as_label(survey_dat$DEM.COR.1.0))
```

The Variable Dictionary used to build the data travels with it as the
`dict` attribute, so the question and item text of every column stay at
hand:

```{r}
survey_dict <- attr(survey_dat, "dict")
unique(survey_dict[
  survey_dict$variable_name == "PHQ.DEP.1.0.2",
  c("variable_name", "item")
])
```

### Labelled Export Findings

While applying the dictionary, `survey_fetch_labelled()` records Labelled
Export Findings: for example, a dictionary column that is missing from the
downloaded data. `survey_export_findings()` returns them. The example has
none:

```{r}
survey_export_findings(survey_dat)
```

### Download options

`survey_fetch_labelled()` calls `qualtRics::fetch_survey()` with the settings
it needs to match columns to `response_column_id`: `import_id = TRUE`,
`label = FALSE`, `convert = FALSE` and `breakout_sets = TRUE`. You may pass
other `fetch_survey()` arguments, such as `include_questions`, but not ones
that override those settings.

By default, variables with Validation Findings stay in the data.
`exclude_findings = "definite"` drops the variables with definite findings,
and `exclude_findings = "validation"` drops every variable with any finding:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
survey_dat <- survey_fetch_labelled(
  dict,
  extra_columns = c("externalDataReference", "startDate", "endDate"),
  exclude_findings = "definite"
)
```

## Survey Block views

`dict_generate()` returns one Variable Dictionary and
`survey_fetch_labelled()` returns one data frame. To work with one Survey
Block at a time, split them. Rows without a block, here the embedded data
fields and scoring variables, are kept under `"..unassigned"`.

```{r}
dict_by_block <- dict_split_blocks(dict)
names(dict_by_block)
unique(dict_by_block$PHQ9[, c("response_column_id", "variable_name")])

data_by_block <- survey_split_blocks(survey_dat)
names(data_by_block)
names(data_by_block$PHQ9)
```

By default each block's data keeps `externalDataReference`, `startDate` and
`endDate` so the blocks can be joined back together.

## Semantic Names

If the Question Names in your survey are not good analysis names, ask for
Semantic Names. They are generated from the question text, block information
and response metadata, and need the suggested packages slowraker, SnowballC,
stringi and tidyr. `block_pattern` turns each Survey Block name into a Block
Prefix, which is prepended to the Semantic Names in that block so that
variables from different blocks stay distinct:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
block_pattern <- function(block) {
  substring(block, 1, 3)
}

dict <- dict_generate(
  survey_id,
  variable_name = "semantic_name",
  block_pattern = block_pattern,
  block_sep = "."
)
```

Semantic Names are best-effort readable conveniences. They are not stable
across package versions or survey text changes, so do not treat them as
permanent identifiers. For long text, Semantic Names select important words
from ranked keywords and keep them in the order they appear in the text.

You can also preprocess the text used only for Semantic Name generation:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
drop_intro_text <- function(dict) {
  dict$question <- sub("^Please answer: ", "", dict$question)
  dict
}

dict <- dict_generate(
  survey_id,
  variable_name = "semantic_name",
  semantic_name_preprocess = drop_intro_text
)
```

`semantic_name_preprocess` receives the full dictionary and runs only on the
Semantic Name path. Temporary helper columns it creates are not included in
the returned Variable Dictionary.

## Learn more

The help page of each function, such as `?dict_generate` or
`?survey_fetch_labelled`, documents its arguments in full.
